chapters.title: Chapter 3: Recession Signals in Real Economy Data

lessons.title: PMI Manufacturing and Services: The Fastest Signal You're Probably Ignoring

body.text: Most commentary reduces PMI to a single question: above or below 50. The genuinely useful information sits one layer deeper, in the new orders sub-index and in where Manufacturing and Services PMI disagree with each other.

children.text: Lesson 3.1 covered IIP and core sector data, both government releases with a real lag between the period measured and the print landing. PMI is different in kind, not just in speed: it is a private survey, compiled from purchasing managers' own assessments of current conditions, which is exactly why it lands within days of month-end rather than weeks. This lesson covers what that survey actually captures, why Manufacturing and Services PMI can and do tell different stories, and why the new orders sub-index deserves more weight than the headline print most coverage quotes.
What PMI Actually Is, and Why It's Released So Fast

S&P Global surveys several hundred purchasing managers each month, asking a simple question across five areas of their business: is this better, the same, or worse than last month. Those five areas, new orders, output, employment, suppliers' delivery times, and stock of purchases, are combined into a single diffusion index using fixed weights, the same diffusion index concept introduced in Lesson 1.2. Because the underlying data is a qualitative survey response rather than a physical volume that has to be measured, collected, and processed the way IIP's is, PMI can be compiled and published almost immediately, typically within the first few business days after the month ends, which is what makes it the fastest genuinely useful economic signal covered in this course.

children.text: Manufacturing vs Services: Two Different Stories

columns.label: Manufacturing PMI
points: More sensitive to global trade conditions and export demand
New export orders sub-component gives a direct read on external demand
Tends to move with global manufacturing and commodity cycles, not just domestic conditions
Historically the more closely watched of the two by global markets

columns.label: Services PMI
points: More sensitive to domestic demand, discretionary spending, and credit conditions
Captures a sector that, per Lesson 1.3, makes up over half of India's GVA and is entirely missed by IIP
Can diverge sharply from Manufacturing PMI when a shock is external (trade, commodity prices) rather than domestic
Tends to be somewhat more volatile month to month than Manufacturing PMI

children.text: This split matters for exactly the same reason the external-versus-domestic distinction mattered in Lesson 2.4's case studies. If Manufacturing PMI is weakening sharply while Services PMI stays firm, that pattern is more consistent with an external shock, a global trade slowdown or commodity disruption hitting export-facing manufacturing, than with a genuine domestic downturn. If both weaken together, and particularly if Services PMI, the larger and more domestically driven of the two, rolls over, that is a stronger signal of broad-based domestic weakness.

body.text: Do not average Manufacturing and Services PMI together in your head and call it a day. A Composite figure that looks merely soft can be hiding a sharp divergence, exactly the kind of pattern worth digging into rather than skipping past, the same discipline Lesson 3.1 applied to IIP's use-based categories.

children.text: The Sub-Index That Matters Most: New Orders

New orders carries the largest single weight in the PMI formula, and it is also the most forward-looking of the five components: it asks about orders already booked for future production, not output that has already happened. That makes it a leading indicator within a leading indicator, structurally similar to how capital goods lead the headline IIP number in Lesson 3.1. A headline PMI still comfortably above 50 can mask a new orders sub-index that has already fallen toward or below 50, precisely the divergence this course keeps asking you to look for one layer beneath the headline. For manufacturing specifically, the new export orders sub-component narrows this further, isolating external demand from the domestic portion of new orders.

body.title: Reading a PMI Release
steps: Check both Manufacturing and Services PMI, not just whichever one the headline you saw led with
Look at the new orders sub-index specifically, and compare its direction to the headline figure
For Manufacturing PMI, check new export orders separately to isolate the external demand component
Note whether employment, the more lagging component, is still rising even as new orders softens, a common early-stage divergence
Cross-check the PMI read against the latest core sector or IIP data from Lesson 3.1 to see whether the two are telling a consistent story

body.title: Read Beneath the Headline
body.scenario: Manufacturing PMI has fallen from 57 to 52 over three months, still comfortably in expansion territory. But the new orders sub-index has fallen further, to 49, and new export orders specifically have dropped to 46. Over the same period, Services PMI has stayed strong at 60, largely unchanged.
body.prompt: What does this combination suggest about whether this is a broad domestic slowdown or something narrower, and what would you watch for next?
body.modelAnswer: This looks like an export-led manufacturing softening rather than a broad domestic slowdown. The headline Manufacturing PMI at 52 still looks expansionary, but new orders at 49 and new export orders at 46 show real weakness building beneath it, concentrated in demand rather than current output, and specifically in the export-facing component given how much further new export orders has fallen than new orders overall. Services PMI holding firm at 60 is the strongest evidence against a broad domestic downturn, since Services PMI is the more domestically driven of the two series from this lesson's framework. The next things to watch are whether Manufacturing new orders keeps falling toward and below 50, which would eventually drag the headline print down too, and whether Services PMI starts softening as well, which would be the signal that this has stopped being an external, manufacturing-specific story and has become a genuine broad-based slowdown.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why can PMI be released so much faster than IIP, often within days of month-end?
options: Because PMI covers a smaller geographic area than IIP
Because PMI is based on qualitative survey responses from purchasing managers, which can be compiled quickly, rather than measured physical output volumes that take weeks to collect and process
Because PMI is calculated by the RBI using real-time banking data
Because PMI only covers a single sub-sector of the economy
body.explanation: PMI's speed comes from its methodology: a survey asking purchasing managers whether conditions are better, the same, or worse than last month can be compiled and published almost immediately. IIP, by contrast, requires collecting and processing actual physical production volumes across the economy, a slower process that is why it lags PMI by several weeks.

body.text: This lesson presents a general framework for reading PMI data, for educational purposes. Component weights are presented as approximate and standard to the PMI methodology broadly, and specific historical figures cited, including the April 2020 record low, are widely reported approximations. Always check S&P Global's current release for exact figures. Nothing here is investment advice.

points: PMI is a survey-based diffusion index, which is what allows it to be released within days of month-end, far faster than government data like IIP
Manufacturing PMI is more exposed to global trade and export demand; Services PMI is more exposed to domestic demand and covers a sector IIP misses entirely
A divergence between Manufacturing and Services PMI helps distinguish an external shock from a genuine domestic slowdown, echoing the external-versus-domestic framework from Lesson 2.4
New orders, the largest-weighted PMI component, is the most forward-looking piece, a leading indicator within a leading indicator, similar to how capital goods lead within IIP
